1373.title: Ignatian imagination
1373.hook: Ignatius of Loyola taught people to pray by stepping into a gospel scene
1373.howItsDone: Christians who pray in the Ignatian way often take a gospel passage, read it slowly, then enter the scene in imagination and end by talking with Jesus; it is commonly practiced on guided retreats with a spiritual director.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cloud of unknowing, and one short word sent up into the dark. Your line was by love, not thought.

Where do you stand when you hear a gospel story? A dusty road. A pregnant young woman is riding, and a man walks beside her, tired, looking ahead for somewhere to stop for the night. There's a servant with them, carrying what they own. Then you notice the servant is you. You're carrying the bag. Your feet hurt. You can hear the animal breathing. This is a set of instructions for prayer, from a Spanish soldier turned seeker named Ignatius of Loyola, who went on to found the Jesuits. Yesterday's book put every image down. Today's teacher picks them all up, and walks in.
screen: `A DUSTY ROAD, A TIRED COUPLE.` → `THE SERVANT IS YOU.` → `INSTRUCTIONS FOR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: You met Ignatius's nightly examen on day one hundred eight. His handbook, the Spiritual Exercises, is a guide for a retreat, usually given by one person to another, and here's how its imagining works. First, build the place. Before praying with a gospel story, Ignatius asks the person to see the setting with the eye of the imagination: how long the road is, how wide, whether it's flat or runs through valleys. He calls this composing the place. It's how the mind stops wandering and arrives somewhere. Second, find the people, and find yourself. In his exercise on the birth of Jesus, he asks the one praying to watch Mary, Joseph, and a servant girl, and to become a small, unworthy servant among them, helping with what they need. Third, use every sense. Later in the day, Ignatius suggests going back over the same scene sense by sense: what you see, what you hear, what you might smell and taste, what you'd touch. Readers call this the application of the senses. Fourth, then talk. Ignatius ends with a conversation, speaking as one friend speaks to another, telling what's on your heart and asking for what you need. The imagination is the door: the scene gets you close enough to speak. Some who pray this way say the story becomes a place they can visit, and that a sore foot or a cold wind does more than a perfect picture.
screen: `FIRST, BUILD THE PLACE.` · `FIND THE PEOPLE, AND FIND YOURSELF.` · `USE EVERY SENSE.` · `THEN SPEAK, AS FRIEND TO FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Choose a short scene: if you pray with the Bible, the road to Bethlehem or a fishing boat at dawn; if not, any story that matters to you. Build the place, find where you stand among the people, and notice one sound, one smell, one thing your hand touches. Near the end, if you pray, speak to someone in the scene, plainly; if not, notice what it stirs.
Ignatian imagination. Praying by stepping into a story: build the place, find yourself in it, use the senses, then speak. From the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius of Loyola. Today's word.
Your line: step into the scene. Close enough to speak. Same time tomorrow.

1374.title: The interior castle
1374.hook: Teresa of Ávila pictured the soul as a castle of many rooms, with God at the center
1374.howItsDone: Catholics and other Christians read The Interior Castle as a guide to growth in prayer, often with a spiritual director; Carmelite communities, the order Teresa reformed, study it closely.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius: praying by stepping into a gospel scene with every sense. Your line was step into the scene.

How do you walk into a house you already live in? A Spanish nun named Teresa of Ávila asked a question like that, and admitted it sounded like nonsense. Her superiors had asked her to write about prayer for the sisters in her convents, and she wasn't sure where to start. So she asked God for help, and, she says, a picture came to her. A castle. Not out on a hill somewhere, but inside every person. Full of rooms. And the strange thing, as she tells it, is that plenty of souls stay out in the courtyard and never go in.
screen: `A HOUSE YOU ALREADY LIVE IN.` → `A PICTURE CAME TO HER.` → `LIVING IN THE COURTYARD.`

segments.voice: Teresa's book is called The Interior Castle, and she builds it on a line of Jesus from John's Gospel: "In my Father's house are many mansions." First, what it's made of. Think of the soul, she says, as a castle made of a single diamond, or of very clear crystal. She divides the book into seven dwelling places, and says each has many rooms of its own. In the very center is the main room, where God lives, and where the most secret things pass between God and the soul. Second, the door. If the soul is the castle, how do you get in? Teresa's answer: the door is prayer and reflection. People who never pray, she says, stay outside in the courtyard, among the snakes and creatures of the outer wall, busy with everything except the castle itself. Third, the layout. Don't imagine the rooms in a straight row, she tells her sisters, like a hallway. Think of a palmetto, a plant with many layers wrapped around a tender center. The journey in is less a march than an unwrapping. Fourth, the room you never leave. Teresa says the room of self-knowledge matters at every stage. Knowing yourself honestly, with your faults, keeps a person humble, however far in they've come. Notice where she puts God: not far off at the end of a long road, but at the center of the person, waiting to be visited.
screen: `A CASTLE OF DIAMOND, WITH GOD AT THE CENTER.` · `THE DOOR IS PRAYER.` · `NOT A HALLWAY: A PALMETTO.` · `THE ROOM OF SELF-KNOWLEDGE.` · then, large: `IN MY FATHER'S HOUSE ARE MANY MANSIONS.`

segments.voice: Notice the courtyard first, the noise near the outer wall: today's errands, messages, worries; don't fight them, just see that they're out there. Then step through a door into one quieter room, a memory or someone you love, and then one more, a little further in. If you pray, rest at the threshold of the center and say nothing; if not, notice how it feels to be further in than the courtyard.
The interior castle. Teresa of Ávila's picture of the soul: a castle of clear crystal with many rooms, God at the center, and prayer as the door. Today's word.
Your line: many rooms. The courtyard was never the whole of the castle. See you tomorrow.

1375.title: The dark night
1375.hook: John of the Cross wrote of a dark night where prayer feels empty and something deeper grows
1375.howItsDone: Christians who meet dryness in prayer often talk it over with a spiritual director, who may draw on John of the Cross to help tell a dark night apart from depression or ordinary discouragement.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's interior castle: a soul of many rooms, with prayer as the door. Your line was many rooms.

For years, morning prayer was the best part of her day. Warm. Easy. Words came. Today, nothing. Not anger, not doubt exactly. Just flat, like chewing paper. Tomorrow, the same. And the next week. She starts to wonder what she's done wrong. Teresa's friend and fellow Carmelite, a friar called John of the Cross, wrote a poem about a night like that, and then a whole book explaining the poem. His surprising claim is that the flatness might not mean something has gone wrong at all.
screen: `IT USED TO BE EASY.` → `TODAY, NOTHING.` → `MAYBE NOTHING'S GONE WRONG.`

segments.voice: John's poem begins on a dark night, with someone slipping out of a quiet house, unseen, to meet the one they love. The night isn't the enemy; later in the poem, it's the guide. His prose book, The Dark Night, explains what that means for prayer. First, the sweetness goes. Beginners, John says, often find prayer full of comfort, and then, for a time, God takes the comfort away. The old ways of praying, with pictures and thoughts, stop working. Second, it isn't every dark mood. He gives signs to tell this night apart from ordinary sadness, or what he calls melancholy. The person finds no pleasure in God's things, but none in other things either. They still care, painfully, about whether they're serving God. And they can't meditate with the imagination the way they used to. Third, what to do. John's advice is gentle: don't strain to force the old feelings back. Rest in peace and quiet, with a simple loving attention, even if it seems like wasting time. Fourth, what grows. In John's reading, the night strips away a love that depended on good feelings, so that something quieter and deeper can grow underneath. Some today say dark night of the soul for any hard time; John's own night is narrower, and he took care to say not every darkness is this one. Hard seasons that weigh on everything deserve a friend, and sometimes a doctor, as well as a prayer. If a weight ever feels like too much, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
screen: `THE NIGHT IS THE GUIDE.` · `THE SWEETNESS GOES.` · `NOT EVERY DARK MOOD.` · `REST IN LOVING ATTENTION.` · then: `IF IT'S HEAVY: 988, OR LOCAL HELP.`

segments.voice: Think of a time when something you loved went flat: a prayer, a friendship, a craft, a job. Don't try to fix it or to feel anything special; just sit beside it, the way you'd sit with a friend who doesn't need advice. If you pray, you can offer the dryness itself, without words; if not, just keep it company.
The dark night. In John of the Cross, a season when prayer goes flat and the old comforts fall away, and something quieter grows underneath. Today's word.
Your line: a dark night. Flat isn't always a sign that something's gone wrong. Rest well.

1376.title: Centering prayer
1376.hook: Thomas Keating and other monks taught a silent prayer with one sacred word
1376.howItsDone: People who practice centering prayer sit in silence with eyes closed, gently returning to a chosen sacred word when they notice thoughts, sometimes in groups that meet in churches and retreat houses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of the Cross and a dark night, when prayer goes flat and something quieter grows. Your line was a dark night.

Monks in a Massachusetts abbey kept meeting young visitors hungry for meditation, some of whom had found it on other paths. The story told about the beginning of centering prayer is that the abbot, Thomas Keating, wondered aloud whether his own Christian tradition had a quiet practice like that, one that could be taught simply, to anyone, outside a monastery. His fellow monks went looking. One of them, William Meninger, found an answer on a shelf, in a book this week has already opened: The Cloud of Unknowing. Out of that search came a way of praying with almost nothing in it.
screen: `YOUNG VISITORS, HUNGRY FOR SILENCE.` → `DOES OUR OWN TRADITION HAVE ONE?` → `AN ANSWER ON A SHELF.`

segments.voice: Centering prayer looks simple, and its teachers say it is. First, the door Jesus names. Keating pointed to a line from the Sermon on the Mount: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." Centering prayer treats the closet as an inner room in the person. Second, the sacred word. You choose one short word, like God, or peace, or love. It isn't a magic sound, and it isn't meant to be repeated constantly like a mantra or the Jesus Prayer. In Keating's teaching, it's a sign of intention: I consent to God's presence and action within me. Third, thoughts. Thoughts will come, and that's no failure. Keating compared them to boats going by on a river. You don't chase them and you don't fight them. When you notice you've climbed aboard one, you return, ever so gently, to the sacred word. Then you let even the word fade. Fourth, consent, the heart of it. Centering prayer doesn't try to produce a feeling, a vision, or a calm mind. It's an act of saying yes, again and again, without words. Keating taught that the fruit shows up later, in ordinary life, not during the prayer itself. Some practice it with a group, and Keating suggested a longer sit than today's, twice a day. The shape is the same at any length: a word, a yes, and a lot of gentle returning.
screen: `ENTER INTO THY CLOSET.` · `ONE SACRED WORD, AS A SIGN.` · `THOUGHTS ARE BOATS ON A RIVER.` · `THE HEART OF IT: CONSENT.`

segments.voice: Choose a short word now: if you pray, a word like God or peace; if not, a word like yes, or open. Let it settle once, quietly, then sit. When you notice you've drifted off on a thought, a plan, a memory, even a good insight, come back gently to the word without scolding yourself, and let it go again; the returning is the practice.
Centering prayer. A silent Christian prayer with one sacred word, used as a sign of consent, and returned to gently whenever thoughts carry you off. Today's word.
Your line: consent. A quiet yes, said again and again, without any words. Until tomorrow.

1377.title: Quaker silence
1377.hook: Quakers gather in silence and speak only when moved, seeking "that of God in every one" (George Fox)
1377.carry: that of god in every one
1377.howItsDone: In unprogrammed Quaker meetings, Friends gather in silence, anyone may stand to speak briefly when moved, and the meeting ends with handshakes; programmed Friends meetings include pastors, hymns and sermons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, centering prayer: one sacred word and a lot of gentle returning. Your line was consent.

Benches facing each other. No altar up front, no pulpit, nobody in robes. People come in, sit down, and say nothing. A long quiet stretch goes by. A cough. A chair creaks. Then a woman near the window stands up, says a few sentences about her father, and sits down again. Nobody replies. The silence closes back over, like water. Then two people shake hands, everyone turns and shakes hands, and that's the service. This is a Quaker meeting for worship, the silent kind. Most of the prayer in these last days has been one person, alone. Here the silence is shared.
screen: `BENCHES FACING EACH OTHER.` → `A WOMAN STANDS, SPEAKS, SITS.` → `A HANDSHAKE ENDS IT.`

segments.voice: Quakers call themselves the Religious Society of Friends; you met their way of meeting on day nine hundred twenty-five. Their founder, an Englishman named George Fox, wrote a letter to fellow ministers that carries today's line. Live in a way that preaches without words, he urges, and then "you will come to walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." First, why silence. As Friends see it, if there is something of God in every person, nobody needs to stand in between. So in the silent kind of meeting there's no planned sermon and no appointed speaker. Friends wait together, listening inward. Second, when someone speaks. Anyone may stand, a child, a visitor, a longtime member, if they feel moved to. Friends call this ministry. It's meant to come out of the silence, not out of a prepared speech, and it's usually short. No one debates it afterward. The silence takes it back. Third, that of God in every one. Notice Fox's word: answering. Not just finding something holy in other people, but responding to it. Friends have read the phrase as a call to treat every person as someone who can hear God directly, which has shaped how they handle disagreement, decisions and conflict. Fourth, not every meeting is silent. Some Quaker meetings have pastors, hymns and sermons; others, like the one in the hook, gather in silence. Both are Quaker. And the handshake? It's simply how a silent meeting knows it's over.
screen: `A LETTER FROM GEORGE FOX.` · `NOBODY STANDS IN BETWEEN.` · `SPEAK ONLY WHEN MOVED.` · `NOT EVERY MEETING IS SILENT.` · then, large: `ANSWERING THAT OF GOD IN EVERY ONE.`

segments.voice: If someone is near you right now, a partner, a roommate, a stranger on the bus, let your silence include them; if you're alone, bring a few people to mind and sit with them as if the bench were facing you. Don't send them advice; just wait together, listening. If a word rises that feels worth saying, you can hold it, since not every word needs to be spoken.

1378.title: The Taizé chants
1378.hook: short, repeated chants from an ecumenical community of brothers in a French village
1378.howItsDone: At Taizé and in Taizé-style services elsewhere, people sing short chants many times over, hear a short Bible reading, and keep a long silence together, often by candlelight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quaker silence: Friends waiting together, speaking only when moved. Your line was that of God in every one.

Ubi caritas et amor. A long, low church, almost dark, with candles on the floor up front and people sitting on the ground, a lot of them young, backpacks against the wall. A line is sung. It ends. It starts again. Same words, same tune. And again. Nobody's in a hurry for verse two, because there isn't one. After a while, people stop reading the words off the sheet. A while longer, and some have their eyes closed. This is evening prayer in Taizé, a small village in France. Yesterday the sound of prayer was silence. Today it's a single line, sung until it stops being something you read and becomes something you know.
screen: `A LOW CHURCH, CANDLES ON THE FLOOR.` → `ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `THE SHEET GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: Taizé is home to a community of brothers, men who live together under vows, founded by a Swiss Protestant known as Brother Roger. From the start it was meant to be ecumenical, a place where Christians from different churches could pray together. Today the brothers come from Protestant and Catholic backgrounds, and young people come to spend a week living and praying with them. First, the chants are short: often a single line, sometimes just a few words, some taken straight from scripture or from old prayers. Second, they repeat, sometimes for several minutes. The repetition is the point. Once nobody has to think about the next verse, attention can go somewhere else. Third, the languages. The chants are sung in many languages, including Latin, some of them very old words in new music. Ubi caritas is an old Latin hymn text: "Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est," where charity and love are, God is there. Others echo the Psalms, like Psalm 117: "O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people." Fourth, the silence in the middle. A Taizé prayer usually has a Bible reading and then a long silence, set among the chants. The brothers have said they hope a chant keeps going after the prayer ends, hummed under the breath while working or walking. That's how a short line becomes a companion for the day.
screen: `SHORT: OFTEN A SINGLE LINE.` · `REPEATED UNTIL IT SINKS IN.` · `MANY LANGUAGES, OLD WORDS.` · `A SILENCE IN THE MIDDLE.` · then, large: `UBI CARITAS ET AMOR, DEUS IBI EST.`

segments.voice: Choose one line: if you pray, Ubi caritas, or any short line you already know from your own tradition; if not, a single line of any song that steadies you. Hum or sing it softly, let it end, and start it again, same tune, same words. By the third or fourth time, notice whether you're still reading it in your head, or just singing it.
The Taizé chants. Short lines, often from scripture or old prayers, sung over and over at the ecumenical community in Taizé, with silence in the middle. Today's word.
Your line: sing it again. No verse two needed. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.

1379.title: The Divine Office
1379.hook: monks stop whatever they're doing to pray at set hours, day and night
1379.howItsDone: Monks and nuns gather in church at set hours to sing psalms and prayers; Catholics also pray the Liturgy of the Hours from a breviary or app, and Anglicans pray Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Taizé chants: one short line, sung until it sinks in. Your line was sing it again.

Deep in the night, a bell rings in a monastery. Doors open along a dark corridor. Men in robes walk to the church, some still blinking, and begin to sing psalms. A few hours later, at first light, the bell again. Early morning, again. Midmorning. Midday. Midafternoon. Sunset. And once more before sleep. A brother could be kneading bread, halfway through a sentence in a book, or up a ladder fixing a gutter. When the bell rings, he stops. The day isn't organized around meals or work or meetings. It's organized around prayer, and everything else fits into the gaps.
screen: `A BELL IN THE NIGHT.` → `AGAIN, AND AGAIN, ALL DAY.` → `EVERYTHING ELSE FITS IN THE GAPS.`

segments.voice: The Divine Office is the round of prayer at set hours, made mostly of psalms, that Christian monks, and others too, keep through the day and night. First, a verse. The Psalms speak of praying by the clock: "Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments." And: "At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee." Second, a rule. Benedict of Nursia, whose Rule you met on day eight hundred ninety, wrote it for monks, and it is still followed in monasteries today. He takes those two verses at their word: seven times in the day he sets an hour of prayer, and once in the night, the night office. In his rule, all the psalms are sung through each week. Third, the bell. When the signal for prayer sounds, Benedict says, a monk should put down whatever is in his hands and come at once, though calmly, without rushing about. He calls the prayer the work of God, and says nothing is to be put before it. Fourth, beyond the monastery. Catholics call it the Liturgy of the Hours, and priests, religious and lay people pray it. Anglicans pray Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer. Orthodox Christians keep their own cycle of hours. This week brought a scene stepped into, a castle, a dark night, one sacred word, shared silence, a sung line: ways to pray. The Office is a way to keep praying, by giving the day a skeleton and hanging everything else on it.
screen: `A VERSE: SEVEN TIMES A DAY.` · `A RULE: BENEDICT SETS THE HOURS.` · `THE BELL: PUT IT DOWN AND COME.` · `BEYOND THE MONASTERY.` · then, large: `SEVEN TIMES A DAY DO I PRAISE THEE.`

segments.voice: Put down whatever is in your hands and let them rest, as if this sit were the first of three set hours in your day. If you pray, you can say a line from a psalm you know; if not, breathe and notice the hour: the light in the room, the sounds, what this part of the day is like.
The Divine Office. The round of psalms and prayers kept at set hours of the day and night, which Benedict called the work of God. Today's word.
Your line: the hours. Put it down and come, calmly. A week of ways to pray behind you.
